messages.subject: Mixture model problem
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to fit a simple mixture model, following the instructions in the User guide, but am getting R-hats that are too large. 

Here is the data:

set.seed(96785423)
mu1<-3
mu2<-0
s<-1
y1<-rnorm(1000,mean=mu1,sd=s)
y2<-rnorm(1000,mean=mu2,sd=s)
y<- c(y1,y2)
hist(y,freq=FALSE)

Here is the output from the package mixtools, which uses EM:

> mixmod <- normalmixEM(y, lambda = .5,  ## inits
+                      mu = c(4,2), ## inits 
+                      sigma = 1)
number of iterations= 45 
> summary(mixmod)
summary of normalmixEM object:
         comp 1    comp 2
lambda 0.500924 0.4990761
mu     2.970985 0.0245785
sigma  1.010170 1.0101696
loglik at estimate:  -3886.86 

All parameters recovered correctly.

Here is the Stan model mix1.stan, copied from manual:

data {
int<lower=1> K;
int<lower=1> N;
real y[N];
}

parameters {
simplex[K] lambda;
real mu[K];
real<lower=0> sigma[K];
} 

model {
  real ps[K];
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  mu ~ normal(0, 10);
  for (i in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K) {
      ps[k] = log(lambda[k]) 
              + normal_lpdf(y[i] | mu[k], sigma[k]);
    }
    target += log_sum_exp(ps);
  }
}


And here is the R code to run the model:

dat<-list(y=y,N=length(y),K=2)

library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

## test code:
option<-stanc("mix1.stan")
## run code:
fit<-stan(file="mix1.stan",data=dat,iter=10000)

Output:

 print(fit,probs=c(0.025,0.975))
Inference for Stan model: mix1.
4 chains, each with iter=10000; warmup=5000; thin=1; 
post-warmup draws per chain=5000, total post-warmup draws=20000.

              mean se_mean   sd     2.5%    97.5% n_eff  Rhat
lambda[1]     0.51    0.02 0.03     0.44     0.57     4  1.42
lambda[2]     0.49    0.02 0.03     0.43     0.56     4  1.42
mu[1]         2.16    0.90 1.28    -0.13     3.02     2 19.10
mu[2]         0.69    0.90 1.27    -0.17     2.99     2 19.59
sigma[1]      1.04    0.03 0.06     0.91     1.15     4  1.43
sigma[2]      0.99    0.03 0.06     0.89     1.13     3  1.47
lp__      -3889.95    0.02 1.61 -3893.94 -3887.83  8153  1.00

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
parts:
Hi Shavran,

Take a look at the traceplots or histograms of the parameters. You're getting label switching!

The way your model is specified, mu1 and mu2 should have the same distribution. What's happening is that within a chain, it's not mixing between the two modes, but from different starting points it will find separate modes. In theory, if you ran the algorithm, the chain should mix if you wait long enough. 

In practice, you can make the mus non-exchangeable. If you make them ordered, it should make this problem go away. Or if you add a prior just to help identify one of the mus. 

Hopefully that makes sense. 



Daniel

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
parts:
Just a couple more points:
- the two modes here lead to the same log probability. If you used optimization, it should find one of two modes and you'd get a similar answer to the other program. (If you ran it multiple times, it should bounce between modes)
- this label switching non-identifiability in the model is the same as the one for latent Dirichlet allocation, just much simpler. Bayesian inference over the model as written isn't exactly what you want. I think in practice, you can order the parameters and get an identified model (which is different than what you've written) and get results that make sense.

Daniel

Yes, either replace "real mu[K]” with “ordered[K] mu” to select a single unique
labeling or place informative priors on each mu[k] so that each mixture
component has a specified responsibility.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
parts:
Just curious. I have a quick question about mixtures, and thought I'd piggy back off this, since it's a simple example.

If you wanted to allow individuals differing probabilities of 'belonging' to one component or another, would you estimate per-individual probabilities with a hierarchical prior? I've done this, but I never see others do it, so I'm worried I'm in the wrong.

That is, instead of simplex[K] lambda, could you have:
simplex[K] lambda[N]; // N = number of individuals
for(n in 1:N){
lambda[n] ~ dirichlet(params here);
}

or, in the simpler case of K=2:
vector[N] lambda_logit;
vector[N] lambda_logit_mu;
lambda_logit_mu = some + latent + class + predictors;
lambda_logit ~ logistic(lambda_logit_mu, 1); //And how do you choose the error to this? 1? 3? estimate it?

Mainly, I'm just curious, because when specifying mixtures in, e.g., gibbs using a non-marginalized approach, each individual's membership may be ~ categorical(.2,.3,.5), but p(k_i = 1 | ...) = .8 (not .2).
Yet when using a marginalized model, you aren't estimating p(k_i = 1|D), but the parameters to the categorical prior (so to speak); so how can you obtain p(k_i = 1 | D) from a model that only estimates the prior?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
parts:
You aren't getting the kind of data you need to fit
that simplex, even hierarchically. You only get
one observation and you have (K-1) free parameters.
And it's not like you have overdispersion or something
to fit---you still are just selecting a single group
for membership.

What people often do is have some predictors that
effect membership and instead of a simplex, they
build a multi-logit regression (or a logit if there
are only two categories). For example, in the movement
HMM models in ecology, the probability of an animal
being in a state can depend on time of day, distance
to water, previous movements, etc.

- Bob

> simplex[K] lambda[N]; // N = number of individuals
> for(n in 1:N){
> lambda[n] ~ dirichlet(params here);

>
> or, in the simpler case of K=2:
> vector[N] lambda_logit;
> vector[N] lambda_logit_mu;
> lambda_logit_mu = some + latent + class + predictors;
> lambda_logit ~ logistic(lambda_logit_mu, 1); //And how do you choose the error to this? 1? 3? estimate it?
>
> Mainly, I'm just curious, because when specifying mixtures in, e.g., gibbs using a non-marginalized approach, each individual's membership may be ~ categorical(.2,.3,.5), but p(k_i = 1 | ...) = .8 (not .2).
> Yet when using a marginalized model, you aren't estimating p(k_i = 1|D), but the parameters to the categorical prior (so to speak); so how can you obtain p(k_i = 1 | D) from a model that only estimates the prior?

Ok, so lets assume you have K=2 latent groups, and you're parameterizing via logits (which is what I tend to do).

If you don't have latent group predictors, and you want to fit a mixture (in essence, an intercept-only model), then the manual's method is the way you'd go; you don't estimate pi_logit[n] for each person, but pi_logit as a prior; then you convert to pi, then use that to compute a posterior probability of group membership?
E.g., for(n in 1:N){ target += log_mix(pi, lpdf(y[n] | params[1]), lpdf(y[n] | params[2]) }; then later, you compute simplex[2] pi_n[N] manually, by solving for p(k=2 | y_i)?

If you *do* have latent group predictors, and you want to fit a mixture, then you CAN estimate pi_logit[n] for each person, and put the converted pi straight into the likelihood?
E.g., for(n in 1:N){ target += log_mix(pi[n], lpdf(y[n] | params[1]), lpdf(y[n] | params[2]) }; where logit(pi[n]) = some + latent + group + predictors; then you manually compute p(k = 2 | y_i) as above?

I... think I have some work to do on my model. This may actually solve a major identifiability issue in my model.

TLDR; I was conceptually fitting a per-person likelihood that is: pi[n]*f(y[n] | params[1]) + (1 - pi[n])*f(y[n] | params[2]); logit(pi[n]) ~ logistic(pi_predicted[n], 1), and using pi[n] as posterior membership probability, and pi_predicted[n] as either the overall "prior" membership logit (if intercept-only model) or predicted membership probability.

Instead of: pi*f(y[n] | params[1]) + (1 - pi)*f(y[n] | params[2]); then manually computing posterior membership probability by solving for p(k = 2 | y_i) = p(y_i | k = 2)p(k = 2) / (sum_k^2(p(y_i | k)p(k))
I think I can use this ^^, and still predict pi[n] (using logit modeling), but it will need to be deterministic (no ~ logistic(pi_predicted[n]); instead you fit the model and still manually compute the posterior membership prob.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
parts:
> On Jan 31, 2017, at 2:03 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Ok, so lets assume you have K=2 latent groups, and you're parameterizing via logits (which is what I tend to do).
>
> If you don't have latent group predictors, and you want to fit a mixture (in essence, an intercept-only model), then the manual's method is the way you'd go; you don't estimate pi_logit[n] for each person, but pi_logit as a prior; then you convert to pi, then use that to compute a posterior probability of group membership?

> E.g., for(n in 1:N){ target += log_mix(pi, lpdf(y[n] | params[1]), lpdf(y[n] | params[2]) }; then later, you compute simplex[2] pi_n[N] manually, by solving for p(k=2 | y_i)?
Yes, see below.

> If you *do* have latent group predictors, and you want to fit a mixture, then you CAN estimate pi_logit[n] for each person, and put the converted pi straight into the likelihood?
> E.g., for(n in 1:N){ target += log_mix(pi[n], lpdf(y[n] | params[1]), lpdf(y[n] | params[2]) }; where logit(pi[n]) = some + latent + group + predictors; then you manually compute p(k = 2 | y_i) as above?
Exactly.

> I... think I have some work to do on my model. This may actually solve a major identifiability issue in my model.
>
> TLDR; I was conceptually fitting a per-person likelihood that is: pi[n]*f(y[n] | params[1]) + (1 - pi[n])*f(y[n] | params[2]); logit(pi[n]) ~ logistic(pi_predicted[n], 1), and using pi[n] as posterior membership probability, and pi_predicted[n] as either the overall "prior" membership logit (if intercept-only model) or predicted membership probability.
>
> Instead of: pi*f(y[n] | params[1]) + (1 - pi)*f(y[n] | params[2]); then manually computing posterior membership probability by solving for p(k = 2 | y_i) = p(y_i | k = 2)p(k = 2) / (sum_k^2(p(y_i | k)p(k))
> I think I can use this ^^, and still predict pi[n] (using logit modeling), but it will need to be deterministic (no ~ logistic(pi_predicted[n]); instead you fit the model and still manually compute the posterior membership prob.

If we let the density for each mixture component be

ps[1, n] = pi * f(y[n] | params[1])

ps[2, n] = (1 - pi) * f(y[n] | params[2])

then we have

Pr[z[n] = 1] = ps[1, n] / (ps[1, n] + ps[2, n])

or more stably,

log Pr[z[n] = 1] = log ps[1, n] - log_sum_exp(ps[1, n], ps[2, n]))

where, e.g.,

log ps[1, n] = log(pi) + log(f(y[n] | params[1]))

- Bob
